transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-08-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Jordan Miles (CTO - QuantFlux), Priya Nambiar (Platform Eng - QuantFlux), Carlos Ruiz (SRE - QuantFlux)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Discussed hosting options and p95 targets; action items around pricing, benchmarks and security review.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Ethan our systems SE.
[00:08] Jordan Miles: Hi, Jordan here. Thanks, Maya. We wanted to walk through the hosting options, mainly because we have pretty tight p95 latency goals for streaming.
[00:15] Priya Nambiar: Yeah hi, Priya as well. We're serving real-time assistant responses inside our trading desk UI, so p95 matters.
[00:22] Ethan Brooks: Got it. Can you share the p95 numbers you're trying to hit and what your concurrency looks like?
[00:28] Jordan Miles: Sure. Our target is p95 <= 300ms for turn-level streaming (first token to first byte ideally) and end-to-end generation p95 under 1.2s for 512-token outputs. Concurrency expected in steady state around 40 streams, peaks up to 75, token/sec per stream roughly 80-140 depending on prompt.
[00:47] Carlos Ruiz: And we have burst windows - market open - where token requests spike, so cold starts and queueing are our worry.
[00:54] Maya Chen: Makes sense. We normally talk through Hosted, Dedicated and Private tradeoffs. Hosted is fastest time-to-value and we have multi-tenant optimizations, Dedicated gives you isolated pools and predictable throughput, Private lets you run in your VPC or on-prem with your KMS.
[01:12] Jordan Miles: For compliance reasons we might need Private, but we want to understand cost delta and whether Dedicated could meet p95 with the right routing.
[01:21] Ethan Brooks: Quick note: streaming p95 is sensitive to both kernel latencies and network tail. For short turns the runtime's token emission path matters a lot. We optimize for continuous batching and KV cache stays hot to avoid re-encode costs.
[01:36] Priya Nambiar: Sorry, can you explain KV cache warm-up? We saw references to K-V cash in some notes —
[01:42] Ethan Brooks: Yeah, sorry bad transcript there, KV cache — key-value cache for the transformer past key values. If the cache is warm for a conversation we avoid recomputing prior context which reduces per-token compute. Cold conversations can add tens to hundreds of ms depending on model size and quantization.
[01:58] Jordan Miles: Do you have examples numbers for a 70B model versus a 13B quantized variant?
[02:05] Ethan Brooks: Ballpark: on A100-class infra a 13B quantized path with optimized kernels can hit 80-120 tokens/sec sustained and sub-200ms per-token tail in many cases; 70B generally will be slower and more variable, maybe 20-35 tokens/sec depending on quantization and kernel selection. But these are broad numbers - we'll run your exact benchmark.
[02:26] Carlos Ruiz: What's the breakout between network and GPU on that sub-200ms claim? We see some network jitter in us-east during spikes.
[02:33] Ethan Brooks: Good question. For streaming first-byte latency often the emission pipeline and CPU-to-GPU marshalling are dominant. Network tail is real — we can add local egress routing (region pinning) and edge proximity. For Dedicated you can reduce co-tenancy noise.
[02:50] Maya Chen: Also important: we support automatic fallback to smaller quantized variants when there's pressure so you don't hit hard throttles; that's a policy you can set per route.
[02:59] Priya Nambiar: That fallback, is it seamless for clients? Like do we get partial result or does it change tokenization?
[03:05] Ethan Brooks: It's seamless at the API level; the output might change slightly since it's a different model variant, so we recommend canarying and running evals on critical prompts. Redwood Optimize can suggest which prompts are sensitive.
[03:18] Jordan Miles: Ok. From infra side, what autoscale latency do you see when spinning new Dedicated workers? Minutes? Seconds?
[03:26] Ethan Brooks: Our Dedicated autoscale can add warm workers within 30-90s depending on GPU provisioning and your chosen policy. For very quick spikes we recommend reserved headroom or burst capacity configuration, or a mix: Dedicated with small reserve and Hosted fallback.
[03:41] Carlos Ruiz: So for market open spikes we'd want reserved capacity to avoid that autoscale window. How does pricing look for reserved vs pure on-demand?
[03:49] Maya Chen: We'll share a simple cost model but in short reserved (monthly commit) is ~30-50% cheaper per token for steady throughput; on-demand is higher but gives elasticity. Mixed model allows you to cap committed cost and burst into Hosted.
[04:04] Priya Nambiar: On security: we need SOC2 level logs, SSO with SAML, integration with our KMS for key rotation, and auditability for inference inputs. Can Private meet all that?
[04:15] Maya Chen: Yes. Redwood Private gives you a customer-managed control plane option. It integrates with your KMS/HSM, supports SAML SSO, RBAC, and we surface audit logs. We'll bring our security PM to the next call and share our SOC2 package.
[04:29] Jordan Miles: How are logs stored — do you retain request/response payloads by default? We need to be able to disable retention for PII flows.
[04:36] Ethan Brooks: By default Hosted retains minimal telemetry; retention settings are configurable and we can disable payload retention or route logs to your S3 in Private deployments. We also support field-level redaction if you want to avoid storing PII.
[04:49] Priya Nambiar: That helps. For the benchmarking you mentioned — what do you need from us?
[04:55] Ethan Brooks: Ideally a traffic trace: distribution of prompt lengths, typical context size, concurrency sketch and a small sample prompt set to use for fidelity regressions. Also whether you prefer to test against Hosted or Dedicated capacity.
[05:07] Jordan Miles: We'll send sample traces. Can you run a 24-hour token/sec run to capture diurnal and cold-start characteristics?
[05:14] Ethan Brooks: Yes we can. We'll run both sustained and burst scenarios, and capture p95 for first-byte and full-generation. We'll include KV cache warm/cold runs.
[05:24] Carlos Ruiz: One more on quantization — are you offering int8 or int4 paths? How does that affect quality?
[05:30] Ethan Brooks: We support quantization-aware kernels; int8 is common and preserves quality for many models; int4 can further reduce cost but some prompts may show degradation. Redwood Optimize will flag sensitive prompts and suggest the right quantization profile.
[05:44] Priya Nambiar: Any known issues with streaming while quantized? We need streaming continuity for partial responses.
[05:49] Ethan Brooks: Usually fine — the runtime's emission pipeline is orthogonal to quantization, but quantized kernels can sometimes introduce variability under high concurrency; we'll include that in the report.
[05:59] Jordan Miles: Ok, let's talk SLA. We need SLOs around uptime and latency for production. What's Redwood's SLA for Dedicated?
[06:07] Maya Chen: Dedicated can have SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in enterprise contracts; we can put p95 latency targets into the SLA for the reservation term depending on observed benchmarks and agreed routing policies.
[06:18] Jordan Miles: Great. For integration, our client stack uses gRPC streaming and we have connection multiplexing. Any gotchas?
[06:25] Ethan Brooks: gRPC streaming is supported; connection reuse helps reduce TLS overhead so keep that. Multiplexing multiple logical conversations over a single connection is fine but watch per-connection token throughput limits; we'll include guidance.
[06:38] Priya Nambiar: Is there a recommended approach for prefix caching since we have lots of repeated system prompts?
[06:44] Ethan Brooks: Yes, prefix caching at the request layer combined with KV cache on the runtime is effective. You can pre-warm KV cache for high-value sessions using a keepalive traffic pattern or a background warm process.
[06:55] Jordan Miles: Any hidden costs we should be aware of? E.g., egress or S3 logs storage?
[07:00] Maya Chen: Egress is standard cloud egress; logs storage if routed to your bucket will be your storage costs. Token compute is the main cost; cache-hit rates and quantization dramatically influence unit cost.
[07:10] Carlos Ruiz: Let's capture the benchmark matrix you plan to run.
[07:13] Ethan Brooks: We'll run: steady-state at concurrency 40 and 75, burst ramp from 10->75 over 60s, cold-start windows with empty KV cache, quantized vs full precision variants, and streaming first-byte p95 and end-to-end p95 for typical prompt lengths.
[07:29] Priya Nambiar: Nice. Also include a multi-region failover scenario with routing to fallback region.
[07:34] Ethan Brooks: Will do.
[07:36] Jordan Miles: Sounds good. One last thing — how do you surface per-token cost over time in your console? We need to tie token costs to routes and models.
[07:45] Maya Chen: The Redwood Console gives per-route and per-model token cost breakdowns with token-level latency. You can export granular CSVs and set alerts for cost regressions.
[07:55] Priya Nambiar: Perfect.
[07:58] Maya Chen: Ok quick recap — action items: Maya will send pricing and a simple cost model; Ethan will run the 24h benchmarks with our sample prompts; Jordan will send traffic traces and prompt set; we'll schedule a security deep-dive focused on Private with our security PM. Anything else?
[08:14] Jordan Miles: No, that's it. Thanks everyone.
[08:17] Carlos Ruiz: Thanks.
[08:19] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up by email with links to the benchmark plan and a calendar invite for the security review.
